course.title: C# Fundamentals: From First Line to Object-Oriented Thinking
course.description: A complete beginner's journey into C# and .NET. Covers syntax, data types, control flow, object-oriented programming, exception handling, and file I/O. Designed for absolute beginners who want to build a solid foundation in modern C# development.

blocks.value: What is C# and Where is it Used?

C# (pronounced 'C Sharp') is a modern, object-oriented, type-safe programming language developed by Microsoft. It runs on the **.NET runtime**, a managed execution environment that handles memory, security, and performance. C# is used for web apps (ASP.NET), desktop apps (WPF, WinForms), mobile apps (MAUI), games (Unity), cloud services, and AI/ML workloads. Its syntax is similar to Java, C++, and JavaScript, making it an excellent language to learn as a foundation.

blocks.output:
Hello, C# World!
Today is: 7/23/2026

blocks.question: What runtime environment executes C# code?
blocks.explanation: C# compiles to Intermediate Language (IL) which is executed by the Common Language Runtime (CLR), part of the .NET ecosystem.

parts.partTitle: Part 2: Your First Program, Syntax & Project Structure

blocks.value: Program.cs, Namespaces, Statements, and Semicolons

C# is a statically typed language with a strict syntax. Every statement ends with a semicolon (`;`). Code is organized into **namespaces** (to avoid naming conflicts) and **classes** (containers for logic). The entry point of any console application is the `Main` method. In modern C# (top-level statements), you can write code directly without the boilerplate, but understanding the full structure is essential.

blocks.output:
Welcome to C#
Enter your name: Alice
Hello, Alice!

blocks.question: Which method serves as the entry point (starting point) of a C# console application?
blocks.explanation: The `Main` method is where execution begins. It can be written as `static void Main(string[] args)` or simplified in top-level programs.

parts.partTitle: Part 3: Variables, Data Types & Type Conversion

blocks.value: Declaring Variables, Built-in Types, and Casting

Variables in C# must declare their type (or use `var` for implicit typing). Common types: `int` (whole numbers), `double` (decimals), `decimal` (precise financial calculations), `bool` (true/false), `char` (single character), and `string` (text). Use **explicit casting** `(int)value` when you know the conversion is safe, and **`Convert.ToInt32()`** or **`int.Parse()`** for string-to-number conversions. **`TryParse()`** is the safest way to convert user input.

blocks.output: Age: 25, Price: 19.99, Parsed: 42, Safe: False

blocks.question: Which method safely attempts to convert a string to an integer without throwing an exception if it fails?
blocks.explanation: `int.TryParse()` returns a boolean indicating success and outputs the converted value via an `out` parameter. It never throws a format exception.

blocks.value: Arithmetic, Comparison, Logical, and Assignment Operators

Operators perform actions on values. **Arithmetic** operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`) handle math. The `%` (modulo) gives the remainder. **Comparison** operators (`==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`) return booleans. **Logical** operators (`&&` for AND, `||` for OR, `!` for NOT) combine conditions. **Assignment** operators (`=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`) update variables. The **ternary operator** `? :` provides a shorthand for simple if/else assignments.

blocks.output:
Sum: 13
Divide: 3
Modulo: 1
Float divide: 3.333...
Score: 20, Status: Pass

blocks.question: What is the result of `10 / 3` when both operands are integers in C#?
blocks.explanation: In C#, dividing two integers performs integer division, which truncates (cuts off) the decimal part. To get a decimal result, cast one operand to double: `(double)10 / 3`.

blocks.value: Working with Text in C#

Strings in C# are immutable sequences of characters. Use **string interpolation** (`$"Hello {name}"`) for readable concatenation. The `String` class provides powerful methods: `ToUpper()`, `ToLower()`, `Trim()`, `Substring()`, `Replace()`, `Split()`, and `Contains()`. For building strings in loops (where immutability causes performance issues), use **`StringBuilder`**.

Alice Smith
alice@example.com
Words count: 5
ABCD-****-EFGH
Item 1, Item 2, Item 3, Item 4, Item 5,

blocks.question: Which C# symbol enables string interpolation, allowing variables inside double quotes?
blocks.explanation: Prefixing a string with `$` enables interpolation: `$"Hello {name}"` evaluates the variable `name` and inserts its value into the string.

parts.partTitle: Part 6: Conditional Statements — If, Else If, Else

blocks.value: Making Decisions in Code

Programs need to make decisions. The `if` statement executes code when a condition is true. `else if` checks additional conditions. `else` catches everything else. Conditions must evaluate to a boolean. You can nest conditions, but avoid excessive nesting for readability. Use curly braces `{}` even for single-line blocks to prevent bugs.

blocks.output:
Enter your age: 25
You are an adult.
Access VIP lounge.

blocks.question: Which keyword checks a new condition only if all previous conditions in the chain were false?
blocks.explanation: `else if` is evaluated only when the preceding `if` (and any prior `else if`s) are false. It creates a mutually exclusive decision chain.

parts.partTitle: Part 7: Switch Statements & Pattern Matching Basics

blocks.value: Cleaner Multi-Branch Decisions

When checking one variable against many constant values, `switch` is cleaner than a long `if/else if` chain. Each `case` must end with `break` (or `return`) to prevent fall-through. The `default` case handles unmatched values. Modern C# supports **switch expressions** (C# 8+) for concise assignment.

blocks.output:
Enter a day number (1-7): 5
Friday
Switch expression result: Friday

blocks.question: Which keyword in a switch statement handles any value not matched by previous cases?
blocks.explanation: The `default` case in a switch statement acts as a catch-all, similar to the final `else` in an if-else chain.

parts.partTitle: Part 8: Loops — For, While, Do-While, Foreach

blocks.value: Repeating Actions Efficiently

Loops execute code repeatedly. The `for` loop is count-controlled (best when you know the iteration count). The `while` loop is condition-controlled (best when the count is unknown). The `do-while` loop guarantees at least one execution. The `foreach` loop iterates over collections without managing an index. Use `break` to exit early and `continue` to skip to the next iteration.

T-minus 3...
T-minus 2...
T-minus 1...
Enter password (min 6 chars): hi

Password accepted.

blocks.question: Which loop is best suited for iterating through every item in an array without needing an index counter?
blocks.explanation: `foreach` provides clean, read-only iteration over any collection that implements IEnumerable. It eliminates off-by-one errors and index management.

blocks.value: Storing Multiple Values in Order

An **array** stores a fixed number of elements of the same type. Use `int[] numbers = new int[5];` to declare. Arrays have a fixed length set at creation. For dynamic sizing, use **`List<T>`** from `System.Collections.Generic`. Lists grow automatically and provide methods like `Add()`, `Remove()`, `Contains()`, and `Count`.

blocks.question: Which collection type in C# automatically resizes when you add or remove elements?
blocks.explanation: List<T> wraps an array and automatically manages capacity, resizing internally as elements are added or removed. Standard arrays have a fixed length.

parts.partTitle: Part 10: Methods — Parameters, Return Values & Overloading

blocks.value: Organizing Code into Reusable Blocks

Methods (also called functions) encapsulate logic. They can accept **parameters** (input) and **return** a value (output). Use `void` when no value is returned. **Method overloading** allows multiple methods with the same name but different parameter signatures. The `return` statement exits the method immediately and passes a value back to the caller.

blocks.output:
Welcome, Alice!
Area: 16.5
5
6.0
6
Sending 'No Subject' to alice@example.com
Sending 'Meeting Tomorrow' to bob@example.com

blocks.question: What keyword indicates that a method does not return any value?
blocks.explanation: The `void` return type means the method performs an action (like printing) but does not send a value back to the caller.

blocks.value: The Foundation of Object-Oriented Programming

A **class** is a blueprint for creating **objects**. It defines **fields** (variables that belong to the object) and **methods** (actions the object can perform). An object is an **instance** of a class, created with the `new` keyword. Each object gets its own copy of instance fields. This models real-world entities: a `Car` class with `Color` and `Speed` fields, and `Accelerate()` and `Brake()` methods.

blocks.output:
Toyota accelerated to 30 mph.
Tesla accelerated to 60 mph.
Toyota stopped.
Car 1: 2024 Toyota Corolla

blocks.question: Which keyword creates a new instance (object) from a class blueprint?
blocks.explanation: The `new` keyword allocates memory and invokes the class constructor to create a new object instance: `Car myCar = new Car();`

blocks.value: Encapsulation and Controlled Access

**Properties** provide controlled access to fields using `get` and `set` accessors. **Auto-implemented properties** (`public string Name { get; set; }`) create a hidden backing field automatically. A **constructor** is a special method named after the class that runs when an object is created. **Access modifiers** control visibility: `public` (anywhere), `private` (only inside the class), `protected` (class and subclasses), and `internal` (same project).

blocks.output:
Holder: Alice Smith, Number: ACC-12345
Deposited $250.00. New balance: $1,250.00

blocks.question: Which access modifier restricts a member to be accessible only within its own class?
blocks.explanation: Private members are hidden from all external code, including other classes. This is the core of encapsulation — protecting internal state.

blocks.value: Building Class Hierarchies and Overriding Behavior

**Inheritance** lets a class (child/derived) acquire members from another class (parent/base). Use the `:` symbol. The `base` keyword calls the parent constructor or methods. **Polymorphism** means 'many forms' — a derived class can override a base class method using the `virtual` (base) and `override` (derived) keywords. This enables treating different objects uniformly through their base type.

blocks.output:
Rex says: Woof! Woof!
Whiskers says: Meow!
Some generic animal sound.

blocks.question: Which keyword in a derived class indicates that a method is replacing a base class virtual method?
blocks.explanation: The `override` keyword explicitly replaces the implementation of an inherited `virtual` or `abstract` method in the base class.

blocks.value: Class-Level Data and Named Constants

**Static** members belong to the class itself, not to any instance. Use them for utility methods or shared data (like a counter of all instances). **Constants** (`const`) are compile-time values that never change. **`readonly`** fields can only be set during declaration or in the constructor. **Enums** define named integer constants, making code more readable than magic numbers.

blocks.output:
Order 101 status: Processing
Total orders created: 2
Current tax rate: 8.00%
Created at: 7/23/2026 10:30:15 AM

blocks.question: Which keyword defines a member that belongs to the class itself rather than to any specific instance?
blocks.explanation: Static members are accessed via the class name (`ClassName.Member`) rather than through an object instance. They exist independently of any object creation.

blocks.value: Try, Catch, Finally, and Writing Reliable Code

Exceptions are runtime errors that disrupt normal program flow. C# handles them with `try` (wrap risky code), `catch` (handle specific exceptions), and `finally` (always runs, perfect for cleanup). Catch specific exceptions (`FormatException`, `DivideByZeroException`, `FileNotFoundException`) before catching general `Exception`. Use `throw` to propagate errors. In Visual Studio, use **breakpoints** (F9), **Step Over** (F10), and **Watch windows** to inspect variables during execution.

blocks.output:
Enter a number: 0
Error: Cannot divide by zero.
Execution completed. Cleaning up...
File not found. Creating a default file...

blocks.question: Which block ALWAYS executes, whether an exception occurred or not, and is typically used for cleanup code?
blocks.explanation: The `finally` block executes after try/catch regardless of whether an exception was thrown. It's ideal for closing files, database connections, or releasing resources.

parts.partTitle: Part 16: Namespaces, Using Statements & Code Organization

blocks.value: Structuring Large Projects and Avoiding Name Collisions

As programs grow, you need to organize code into **namespaces** — containers that group related classes. The `using` directive imports a namespace so you don't have to type the full path every time. **Global using** (C# 10+) imports a namespace for the entire project. File-scoped namespaces (C# 10+) reduce indentation by declaring the namespace once at the top of the file.

blocks.output: Product class lives in Models namespace. ProductService in Services namespace imports Models to use the Product type.

blocks.question: Which keyword imports a namespace so its types can be used without fully qualified names?
blocks.explanation: The `using` directive brings a namespace into scope. For example, `using System;` allows you to write `Console` instead of `System.Console`.

parts.partTitle: Part 17: Value Types vs Reference Types

blocks.value: Structs, Classes, and the Stack vs Heap

C# divides types into **value types** and **reference types**. Value types (`int`, `double`, `bool`, `char`, `struct`, `enum`) store their data directly and are copied by value. Reference types (`class`, `interface`, `array`, `string`, `delegate`) store a reference (pointer) to the data on the heap — assignment copies the reference, not the object. This distinction affects memory usage, performance, and behavior when passing variables to methods.

blocks.output:
p1.X = 10, p2.X = 99
person1.Name = Bob
number after method: 5
refPerson.Name after method: Modified

blocks.question: When you assign one class variable to another (`a = b`), what is actually copied?
options: A reference (memory address) pointing to the object
A shallow copy of all properties
blocks.correctAnswer: A reference (memory address) pointing to the object
blocks.explanation: Classes are reference types. The variable holds a reference to the heap memory location. Assignment copies this reference, so both variables point to the same object.

parts.partTitle: Part 18: Null Safety, Nullable Types & Null-Coalescing

blocks.value: Handling Absent Values Safely

Reference types can be `null` (no object). Value types normally cannot. **Nullable value types** (`int?`, `double?`, `bool?`) allow value types to represent missing data. The **null-coalescing operator** `??` returns the left side if not null, otherwise the right side. The **null-conditional operator** `?.` safely accesses members without throwing `NullReferenceException`. C# 8+ introduces **nullable reference types** with compiler warnings to prevent null bugs at compile time.

blocks.output:
Name length: 0
Display: Anonymous
No score available.
Safe score: 0

blocks.question: Which operator returns the left operand if it is not null, otherwise returns the right operand?
blocks.explanation: The null-coalescing operator `??` provides a fallback value. Example: `string name = userInput ?? "Default";`

blocks.value: Contracts, Abstraction, and Multiple Inheritance

An **interface** defines a contract — a set of methods and properties that implementing classes must provide. A class can implement **multiple interfaces**, which simulates multiple inheritance. An **abstract class** is a partially implemented base class that cannot be instantiated directly. It can contain both abstract methods (must override) and concrete methods (shared implementation). Use interfaces when different classes share a capability; use abstract classes when classes share an 'is-a' relationship and common code.

blocks.output:
Alice clocked in at 2:45 PM
Alice is writing code.
Pay: $2,000.00

blocks.question: Which construct allows a class to inherit implementation code while also enforcing method overrides?
blocks.explanation: Abstract classes can contain both implemented methods (shared code) and abstract methods (must be overridden by derived classes). Interfaces only define contracts until C# 8 default implementations.

blocks.value: List<T>, Dictionary<K,V>, and Writing Your Own Generic Methods

Generics allow you to write type-safe, reusable code without boxing/unboxing overhead. Instead of writing separate methods for `int`, `string`, and `double`, write one method with a type parameter `T`. The compiler enforces type safety at compile time. Common generic collections: `List<T>` (ordered list), `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` (key-value map), `HashSet<T>` (unique items), and `Queue<T>` / `Stack<T>`.

Names count: 4

Repository has 1 items.

blocks.question: Which generic collection stores key-value pairs with fast lookup by key?
blocks.explanation: Dictionary uses a hash table internally, providing O(1) average-time complexity for lookups, insertions, and deletions by key.

blocks.value: Type-Safe Function Pointers and the Observer Pattern

A **delegate** is a type that represents references to methods with a specific signature. It enables passing methods as arguments and implementing callback patterns. The **Event** model builds on delegates to implement the **Observer pattern** — objects can subscribe to notifications and react when something happens. Use the built-in `Action<T>` (no return) and `Func<T, TResult>` (returns value) delegates for common scenarios instead of defining custom ones.

blocks.question: Which built-in delegate type represents a method that returns no value (void)?
blocks.explanation: `Action<T>` is a built-in delegate for methods with up to 16 parameters that return void. `Func<T, TResult>` is used when a return value is needed.

blocks.value: Concise Syntax for Queries and Transformations

**Lambda expressions** (`=>`) provide a compact way to write anonymous methods inline. They are the foundation of **LINQ (Language Integrated Query)**, which allows querying collections using SQL-like syntax directly in C#. LINQ methods like `Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, `FirstOrDefault`, and `Any` work on any `IEnumerable<T>`. LINQ queries can be written in **method syntax** (chaining extension methods) or **query syntax** (declarative SQL-like keywords).

blocks.question: Which LINQ method filters a collection based on a condition?
blocks.explanation: `Where` filters elements based on a predicate (a function returning bool). Only elements where the predicate is true are included in the result.

blocks.value: Reading, Writing, and Managing Files

C# provides rich APIs for file operations in the `System.IO` namespace. Use `File.ReadAllText()` and `File.WriteAllText()` for simple string operations. For large files, use `StreamReader` and `StreamWriter` to process line-by-line without loading everything into memory. Always wrap streams in `using` statements to ensure resources are released. The `Path` and `Directory` classes help with file system navigation.

blocks.question: Which statement ensures that a StreamReader's underlying file handle is closed even if an exception occurs?
blocks.explanation: The `using` statement automatically calls `Dispose()` (which closes the stream) when the block exits, even if an exception is thrown. It is the safest pattern for managing unmanaged resources.

blocks.value: DateTime, TimeSpan, and String Formatting Patterns

`DateTime` represents a specific point in time. `DateTime.Now` is local time; `DateTime.UtcNow` is universal time. `TimeSpan` represents a duration. Use `.AddDays()`, `.AddHours()` for arithmetic. Format dates with standard format strings (`d` for short date, `D` for long date, `t` for short time, `g` for general). `DateOnly` and `TimeOnly` (C# 10+) separate date and time concerns.

blocks.question: Which C# type represents a duration or difference between two DateTime values?
blocks.explanation: `TimeSpan` stores elapsed time (days, hours, minutes, seconds). You get one by subtracting two DateTimes: `TimeSpan diff = end - start;`

parts.partTitle: Part 25: Collections Deep Dive — HashSet, Queue, Stack & More

blocks.value: Choosing the Right Collection for the Job

Different collections solve different problems. `HashSet<T>` stores unique values with O(1) lookups — perfect for deduplication. `Queue<T>` is FIFO (First-In-First-Out) — ideal for task scheduling. `Stack<T>` is LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) — used for undo operations and expression parsing. `SortedList<TKey, TValue>` maintains keys in sorted order. Understanding when to use each collection is key to writing efficient code.

blocks.question: Which collection automatically rejects duplicate values when adding items?
blocks.explanation: HashSet<T> only stores unique elements. Adding a duplicate returns false and the set remains unchanged. It uses hashing for O(1) containment checks.

blocks.value: Non-Blocking Operations and the Task Type

Real applications often wait for slow operations — file reads, database queries, API calls. **Synchronous** code blocks the thread, freezing your app. The `async` and `await` keywords let you write **asynchronous** code that looks synchronous but doesn't block. An `async` method returns a `Task` (void operation) or `Task<T>` (operation with result). Use `await` to pause execution until the task completes, freeing the thread to do other work.

blocks.question: Which keyword pauses execution of an async method until the awaited task completes, without blocking the thread?
blocks.explanation: `await` unwraps a Task and returns control to the caller, allowing the thread to process other work. When the task finishes, execution resumes after the await point.

blocks.value: Working with System.Text.Json

JSON is the universal data format for APIs. .NET includes `System.Text.Json` for converting objects to JSON strings (serialization) and back (deserialization). Use `JsonSerializer.Serialize()` and `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>()`. The `JsonSerializerOptions` class customizes behavior — property naming policies (camelCase), indentation, and ignoring null values. Attributes like `[JsonPropertyName]` map C# properties to different JSON keys.

blocks.question: Which method converts a C# object into a JSON string representation?
blocks.explanation: `JsonSerializer.Serialize(object)` converts a .NET object into a JSON string. The reverse operation is `Deserialize<T>(jsonString)`.

blocks.value: Writing Your First Automated Tests

Testing ensures your code works correctly as it changes. **xUnit** is the most popular testing framework for modern .NET. Tests are methods marked with `[Fact]` (parameterless) or `[Theory]` (data-driven with `[InlineData]`). Use the **Arrange-Act-Assert** pattern: set up inputs, call the method, verify the result. Assertions check expected outcomes: `Assert.Equal()`, `Assert.True()`, `Assert.Throws<T>()`. Run tests via `dotnet test` or your IDE's test runner.

blocks.question: Which xUnit attribute marks a test method that accepts parameters and runs once per data row?
blocks.explanation: [Theory] is paired with data attributes like [InlineData] to run the same test logic with different inputs, reducing code duplication.

parts.partTitle: Part 29: .NET CLI, NuGet Packages & Project Structure

blocks.value: Command-Line Tools and Managing Dependencies

The **.NET CLI** is your command-line companion for building, running, and managing projects. Key commands: `dotnet new` (create projects from templates), `dotnet build` (compile), `dotnet run` (execute), `dotnet test` (run tests). **NuGet** is the package manager for .NET — libraries like Newtonsoft.Json, Entity Framework, and xUnit are distributed as NuGet packages. Add them with `dotnet add package`.

# Create a new console application
dotnet new console -n MyFirstApp
cd MyFirstApp

# Add a NuGet package
dotnet add package Newtonsoft.Json

# Build the project
dotnet build

# Run the application
dotnet run

# Run tests
dotnet test

# Create a solution and add projects
dotnet new sln -n MySolution
dotnet new classlib -n MyLibrary
dotnet sln add MyLibrary/MyLibrary.csproj

# List installed packages
dotnet list package

parts.partTitle: Part 30: Building a Complete Console Application

blocks.value: Task Manager — Bringing It All Together

This final part combines everything you've learned into a real-world console application: a **Task Manager**. It uses classes, lists, file I/O, JSON serialization, exception handling, and LINQ. The app can add tasks, list them, mark them complete, save to a file, and load on startup. This is the bridge from tutorial code to production thinking.

blocks.question: Which principle is demonstrated by the TaskManager class hiding its internal _tasks list and exposing only AddTask, ListTasks, and CompleteTask?
blocks.explanation: Encapsulation hides internal state and implementation details, exposing only a controlled public interface. The private _tasks list cannot be modified directly from outside the class.
